song.title: Ring Out The Bells!
song.author: Mark, Helen and Naomi Johnson
song.summary: If you’re looking for a BIG song for a special Easter celebration, look no further! This modern-day hymn (with screaming guitar) explores the significance of the Resurrection, and encourages all believers to ‘shout it from the rooftops, Jesus is alive!’ The closing section features both harmonies and a big crescendo finish. Enjoy!
song.teachingTips:
• As much of this song is in a low register, ensure the children aren’t tempted to ‘belt’ it out or shout, and use lots of support when moving into head voice for the higher notes at the end of the verses (‘power and resurrection’).
  • The rhythm of the words in the first and fifth lines of each verse will need careful practice. Speak them a couple of times first, in rhythm, before singing them.
  • Listen to the use of dynamics at the end of the song, during the ‘We’re coming alive’ section. Encourage your singers to make the most of this gradual and spine-tingling crescendo.

assembly.title: Eggs Galore!
assembly.description: This assembly explores the symbolism of eggs and their place in Pancake Day, Easter and Passover celebrations.

assembly.title: Good Or Sad Friday?
assembly.description: This assembly explores the emotions of happiness and sadness and reflects on whether Easter is a sad or happy time for Christians.

assembly.title: Easter Message
assembly.description: This assembly uses the idea of code-breaking to help consider the special message of Easter.

resources.title: The Bells, The Bells!
resources.content:
[{"key":"7df66ad1fae169f3","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"
  • To play the notes of a ‘micro’ scale
  • To perform a scale as a round, in groups
","title":"What’s achievable","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/green-star-1614702483w2iKm.png"}},{"key":"33f4cec4d9b7d7f5","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Amplified sound system; backing track; pitched percussion and/or keyboards 

","title":"What you need","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/blue-wrench-16147025258WedI.png"}},{"key":"06f457daa949b949","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Listen carefully to the backing track, particularly the introduction. Can the class hear the bell-like sounds? Now listen to the melody. Can they hear any phrases that might sound like bells? The descending scale in bar 8 ‘Shout it from the rooftops’ sounds a bit like a peal of church bells. Remind the class that a scale is a set of notes that go up and down. Can the children play this ‘micro’ scale of D major (as it is only 6 notes rather than 8) on keyboards, chime bars or glockenspiels? 

","title":"","noMargin":false,"background_color":null}},{"key":"c5625862eed7b3a4","layout":"image","attributes":{"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/MusicActivities/musicactivities-ringoutthebells-1616580357YaP8H.png","title":"","noMargin":false,"background_color":null}},{"key":"55369979a802c389","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

(If you don’t have sets of the above notes use the scale of C but starting at A: A G F E D C. You will get the same effect.)

Can they play the scale together as a class, with each note sounding at the same time? You will need to count them in and keep to a steady pulse. Now, split the class into two groups and have the second group start their scale slightly after the first group, like a round. Decide how many times you are going to repeat the scale. Split into further groups, with each group starting their scale in turn, but overlapping with the other groups. The effect should be something similar to pealing bells. Experiment with the tempo i.e. have some groups performing their scale faster and others slower. 

","title":"","noMargin":false,"background_color":null}},{"key":"f4b33270e61b1123","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

At the end of this song, there is a repeated lyric, ‘We’re coming alive!’. Search online for and listen to After The Rain (1983) by Frank Denyer. The composer was inspired to write this from “experiencing the astonishing transformation of an area of semi-desert, when, after a sustained period of drought, a modest shower totally transformed the barren landscape in a very short time into one exploding with life.” Denyer’s use of sound and instrumentation could inspire similar class compositions on this theme. 

","title":"Listen","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/listen-01-1615991956LRT6z.png"}}]
resources.summary: Using the idea of pealing bells, explore scale passages, playing in groups and in a round.

resources.title: Revelations Dance
resources.content:
[{"key":"7993e3f2ab83b89a","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

This is a useful and informative dance to watch around Easter <\/strong>time. Alvin Ailey (1960) created this three-part dance about African-American history, which depicts the struggle from slavery to freedom. Its story can be interpreted to be more generally about struggle and conflict within oneself, but how holding on to faith<\/strong> can pull you through. The Take Me To The Water <\/em>baptism scene is a good reference when thinking about Easter: the dancers perform as if they are being ‘reborn’, fitting the story of the resurrection. The final section is performed as the dancers rejoice in church. <\/p>\n","title":"","noMargin":false,"background_color":null}},{"key":"ef1cba01667bc607","layout":"video","attributes":{"url":"https:\/\/www.youtube.com\/watch?v=RrPJ4kt3a64","title":"Alvin Ailey's Revelations","noMargin":false,"background_color":null}},{"key":"af267592355beab9","layout":"video","attributes":{"url":"","title":"The dancers discuss what the dance means to them","noMargin":false,"background_color":null}}]

resources.title: The Bells!
resources.content:
[{"key":"eeafdd7b37f77fdb","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Ideal for 1-2 sessions

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"2af14890a6c418c4","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"
  • To identify melodic patterns in songs and music
  • To play melodies on tuned percussion from notation
  • To create music inspired by bell chimes
","title":"What’s achievable","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/green-star-1614702483w2iKm.png"}},{"key":"7f058d645702a1b7","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Tuned instruments (keyboards, chime bars, glockenspiels)

","title":"What you need","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/blue-wrench-16147025258WedI.png"}},{"key":"21be08f0f89a228a","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Peal; church bells; ascending; descending; Westminster Quarters; scale; sequence; pitch; allegro; largo; rallentando; rhythm; dotted minim

","title":"Key vocabulary","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/icons-keyvocab-280x280-27-1620218359Ng3ET.png"}},{"key":"b4f2b114737d08a6","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Begin the lesson with a ‘peal’ of bells! Bells are rung in sequence and each bell must be rung continuously by the same person.

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"3f916b2277fbe4a1","layout":"video","attributes":{"url":"https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MLsGCCQo9rQ","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"af8798c92f69484e","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Discuss how bells have been used throughout history and have many different functions: to wake everyone up, call people for worship and to bring people together to celebrate. In World War II bells were a sound of freedom and were silent until the day they could ring to show the world was at peace.

Listen to the famous ‘Westminster Quarters’ melody that is played by Big Ben in London. Different parts of the melody are played at quarter past, half past, and quarter to the hour in Westminster.

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"8013e1b347dcf554","layout":"video","attributes":{"url":"https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NK_n1ON6HM4","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"06e3c1ade4775564","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Listen carefully to the instrumental track of Ring Out The Bells! or London Bells. Can the class hear the bell-like sounds? Now listen to the melody. Can they hear any phrases that might sound like a peal of church bells? The descending scale in bar 6 ‘Shout it from the rooftops’ in Ring Out The Bells! and ‘Bells are calling people home’ of London Bells sounds a bit like a peal of church bells. In London Bells, the melody used in the opening two lines of the song ‘Now it’s time to rebuild London’ is similar to the Westminster Quarters melody.

Next, try exploring some melodies inspired by bells – you could try one or both of these activities.

Pealing Bells

For Ring Out The Bells!, play the descending scale in bar 8 ‘Shout it from the rooftops’.

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"75be6dbff99c8001","layout":"image","attributes":{"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/MusicCurriculum/MusicCurr-ASSETS/YEAR6/year6-musiccurr-thebells-1640079679Y0jJl.png","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"279de8ba965834ef","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Can the children play this scale on keyboards, chime bars or glockenspiels?

If you don’t have sets of the above notes, use the scale of C but start at A: A G F E D C.

Can they play the scale together as a class with each note sounding at the same time? To help them, tap the steady pulse using a clave.

Next, split the class into two groups and have the second start their scale slightly later than the first group, like a round (e.g. the second group could begin as the first play their third note).

Decide how many times you are going to repeat the scale. Split into further groups, with each group starting their scale in turn, but overlapping with the other groups. The effect should be something similar to pealing bells. Experiment with tempo, i.e. have some groups performing their scale faster and others slower.

Chimes

The opening melody of London Bells uses the following pitches taken from the C major scale:

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"b70ea0cb3ccf8d72","layout":"image","attributes":{"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/MusicCurriculum/MusicCurr-ASSETS/YEAR6/year6-musiccurr-thebells2-1640079680gGYPC.png","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"87c729e19be76e3c","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Can the children play these pitches on keyboard, chime bars or glockenspiels? Working in small groups, ask them to use the pitches to create a new London Bells melody.

Get them to experiment with repetition as well as changing the sequence of pitches. They could:

  1. Repeat the melody and finish on the first note of the scale (C) e.g.
    E C D G   E C D G   E C D G  C
  2. Experiment with the order of the pitches e.g.
    C D G E  C D G E  D E C E  C
  3. Explore tempo. They could play fast (allegro), slow (largo) or include a rallentando (get slower) or an accelerando (get faster).

Once the group has created their melody, can they notate it using letter or staff notation?

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"bda5f2f1824e5f06","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Learn to play the Westminster Quarters! Remind them that each section of the melody is played to announce quarter past, half past and quarter to the hour.

Listen to the melody first and get everyone to clap the rhythm. Discuss the note values and explain that the dotted minim is worth three beats.

Divide the class into groups and give them a tuned percussion instrument (notes E C D G) and a copy of the music. Can they play the melody, following the notation?

For some added fun, you could choose some children to play the relevant section of the melody at different times in the school day! E.g. play the first quarter at 11.15 a.m., the second quarter at 1.30 p.m. and the third quarter at 2.45 p.m.

","title":"Step It Up!","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/u1873-1614695091mFFrP.png"}},{"key":"cce3f00879db96cf","layout":"image","attributes":{"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/MusicCurriculum/MusicCurr-ASSETS/YEAR6/year6-musiccurr-thebells3-1640079680mTNbw.png","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"59a1c21fe5ee3c95","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Find out about bells

Bells are among the oldest and simplest musical instruments in the world, used throughout many of the world’s religions – from Anglican church bells to Shintoist and Buddhist bells. In Roman Catholicism, bells symbolize the voice of God and are used to call people to worship, as well as for ceremonies such as weddings and funerals. In Russian Orthodoxy, enormous bells are used to directly address God. ‘The Bell of Good Luck’ is the largest bell in existence and is kept at a Buddhist temple in Henan, China.

","title":"Branch Out","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/u1874-1614695090s5QJx.png"}},{"key":"090a56716dfffb05","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Composers have also taken inspiration from bells!

Carillon de Westminster was inspired by the Westminster chimes and was written for organ by Louis Vierne in the 1920s. Listen to the music and see if the children can identify the Westminster melody played in many different ways throughout the piece!

","title":"Listen","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/listen-01-1615991956LRT6z.png"}},{"key":"6e488d6c32853bf0","layout":"video","attributes":{"url":"https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4y5xeq9aURY","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"acad25f07352850a","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Or how about listening to La Cathédrale Engloutie (The Sunken Cathedral) by the impressionist composer, Claude Debussy. Can the children hear the ‘bell-like’ chords played throughout the piece? Discuss how musical dimensions such as dynamics are used to conjure up the image of the cathedral. Explain that this music is based on an ancient Breton myth about an underwater cathedral off the coast of an island. It rises up from the sea when the water is clear. The music portrays bells chiming, organ sounds and priests chanting.

","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"8b4a082966e264be","layout":"video","attributes":{"url":"https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p-4qAxZ0F6s","title":"","noMargin":false}},{"key":"60fccd592d45b051","layout":"title-block","attributes":{"title":"Assessment Suggestions","background_color":"#009CCF"}},{"key":"8f85f7540836d878","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"
  • Can they identify and describe melodic patterns in songs and music?
  • Can they play phrases from songs and play them on tuned instruments?
  • Can they play melodies following staff notation?
","title":"","noMargin":false}}]
